name: Nootropic stacks

card.summary: Combinations of cognitive-enhancing supplements and drugs that looksmaxxers use for focus, study and motivation, as part of building the mental side of self-improvement.
card.note: Some stack components are prescription or controlled drugs; supplement products have been found mislabeled.

quick.overview:
A nootropic stack is a combination of substances, from caffeine and L-theanine to racetams, herbal extracts and prescription stimulants, taken together for attention, memory, wakefulness and motivation. In looksmaxxing forums they are discussed under 'IQmaxxing' and study-focus threads, tied to the broader goal of self-improvement rather than directly to appearance.

The appearance link is indirect: people say better focus and energy help them stay consistent with training, school and routines. Reviews of 'smart drugs' in healthy people describe modest, dose-dependent effects for some stimulants and limited evidence for most supplements.
quick.how: Forum users compile lists of substances, ask which to add to a stack, and compare experiences. Common items mentioned include caffeine with L-theanine, omega-3, curcumin, Bacopa, creatine, racetams and wakefulness agents. Some prefer non-prescription items and avoid anything that might affect hormones or hair.
quick.risks: Reviews describe side effects, possible dependence with stimulants and long-term safety gaps for many compounds. Supplements can contain undeclared drugs and be mislabeled, and some components are controlled or prescription-only. People with medical conditions or on medication are generally advised by clinicians to consult a physician.

lead: Nootropic stacks are combinations of cognitive enhancers, often called 'smart drugs', that people take together aiming for better focus, memory, wakefulness or motivation. A stack can be as simple as caffeine paired with L-theanine or as long as a list that mixes herbal extracts, nutrients, racetams and prescription wakefulness agents. The word 'nootropic' was coined in 1972 by the Romanian-born researcher Corneliu Giurgea, who proposed criteria such as enhancing learning and memory with very low toxicity. [1][6]

In looksmaxxing communities, stacks are discussed in study and 'lock in' threads and under the label 'IQmaxxing'. Users list what they already take, ask what to add, and trade views on over-the-counter versus prescription options. [3][4][15] The route to looking better is a chain: steadier concentration and energy are said to help someone keep up with training, sleep, skincare routines and schoolwork, which are the habits that change physique, skin and presentation. [1]

Research on cognitive enhancers in healthy people includes narrative and systematic reviews that describe modest, dose-dependent effects for some stimulants and a mixed picture for supplements and plant extracts. [2][5][7] Medical bodies such as the American Medical Association have discouraged prescribing them to healthy people, and regulators have repeatedly warned about unapproved products sold as supplements. [1]

chain: Stack of supplements or drugs taken for focus and wakefulness
More consistent training, study and self-improvement routines
angle.text: People use stacks to concentrate better and keep up with routines that feed into physique, skin care and school. The effect on appearance runs through habits rather than through any change to the face or body.

paras: There is no globally accepted clinical definition of 'nootropic', and the label covers prescription drugs and dietary supplements alike. [1] Wikipedia groups commonly named substances into central nervous system stimulants (caffeine, modafinil and armodafinil, methylphenidate, nicotine, low-dose amphetamine), cholinergics such as citicoline, racetams such as piracetam and phenylpiracetam, herbs such as Bacopa monnieri and Ginkgo biloba, and nutrients such as omega-3 fatty acids and B vitamins. [1] A 2022 review in Nutrients divided the field into classical nootropics, substances increasing brain metabolism, cholinergic agents and plant extracts. [2]

A 'stack' is the community term for a combination taken together or on the same schedule. Stacks are usually built around a base (often caffeine with L-theanine), with other items added for particular goals such as memory, calm focus, motivation or sleep quality. Commercial sellers also package pre-mixed 'stacks'. [14]

Giurgea, born in Bucharest in 1923 and later based in Belgium, worked as a researcher and scientific counselor at the pharmaceutical company UCB and is credited with synthesising piracetam in 1964. [11][16] He introduced the word 'nootropic' (from Greek roots for 'mind' and 'turning') in 1972 and elaborated it in a 1977 paper with M. Salama. His criteria were enhanced learning and memory, resistance of learned behaviour to disruption, protection against brain insults, improved cortical control, and a lack of sedative or stimulant effects with low toxicity. [1] Wikipedia notes that most compounds now called nootropics do not meet those criteria. [1]

Piracetam gave rise to the racetam family, which includes oxiracetam, aniracetam, pramiracetam and phenylpiracetam. [11] Its legal status varies: it is prescription-only in the United Kingdom and Australia, available over the counter in the Czech Republic and, since 2020, in Hungary, and not approved by the US FDA, which has said piracetam products are unapproved drugs rather than dietary supplements. [1][11] Piracetam was reportedly popular among students as a study aid by 2009. [11]

Stimulant-type wakefulness drugs added to the picture. Modafinil was developed in France in the 1970s by Michel Jouvet and Lafon Laboratories, approved in France in 1994 and in the US in 1998 for sleep disorders. It is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US and has been banned in competitive sport by the World Anti-Doping Agency since 2004. Healthy students, office workers and others have used it off label as a smart drug. [12]

By the mid-2010s, reporting in the US described a commercial nootropics scene in the San Francisco Bay Area. Marketplace reported in January 2017 that companies such as Nootrobox and Nootroo sold pre-made pills to tech and white-collar workers and biohackers, and that Nootrobox had raised funding from investors including Marc Andreessen. [14] Co-founder Michael Brandt described the aim as reframing work as 'a means of self-actualization'. [14] Wider coverage tied stacks to biohacking, the quantified-self movement and the 2011 film Limitless, which Wikipedia lists as exploring the opportunities and threats of such products. [13]

Proponents describe nootropics as tools for sustained attention, memory consolidation for exams, motivation and mood. Common arguments are that combinations act on different pathways, that low-risk items like caffeine with L-theanine or omega-3 are a sensible base, and that stronger prescription agents give a bigger effect. [3][4] Some forum users describe stacks as part of an 'IQmaxxing' project parallel to physical looksmaxxing, aimed at doing better in school or work. [15]

Within these communities there are two recurring camps. One favours over-the-counter supplements and avoids anything prescription or controlled; the other holds that non-prescription stimulants give only a small lift and prefers prescriptions. [4][15] Some users say they avoid items they believe affect hair, growth hormone or IGF-1, linking cognitive goals to their appearance goals. [15]

In forum threads, users post lists of items and ask which to add or remove. Typical entries include caffeine with L-theanine, omega-3 fatty acids, curcumin, Bacopa, creatine, racetams, noopept and modafinil, with replies sharing personal experience rather than controlled data. [3][15] Others take nootropics around exams, and some combine them with habits such as sleep tracking or reduced phone use. Clinicians and researchers generally describe use of prescription items without a prescription as misuse. [5][9]

A 2021 systematic review of university students described healthy students using prescription stimulants and modafinil to increase alertness and concentration, along with non-prescription items such as caffeine, guarana and B vitamins. [9] German survey data summarised on Wikipedia reported that about 70 percent of adults in a 2024 study of more than 20,000 people had used a substance to boost mental performance without a prescription within a year, mostly caffeinated drinks, and about 4 percent had used prescription drugs for that purpose. [13]

A 2022 review in Drugs on 'smart drugs' in healthy people noted that users generally perceive the agents as effective, that efficacy in healthy individuals is uncertain, and that reported improvements are temporary. It also described possible cardiovascular, neurological and psychopathological complications with stimulant-type agents. [5] A 2023 systematic review of plant-derived nootropics, which included 256 human papers, reported that Ginkgo biloba was most relevant for perceptual and motor function, Bacopa for language, learning and memory, ashwagandha for anxiety and social cognition, and caffeine for attention and executive function, while noting inconsistencies that need further research. [7]

Wikipedia's summary of cognitive enhancers reports that most supposed nootropics have only small effects in healthy people, that modafinil maintained wakefulness in sustained sleep deprivation without helping attention or executive function, and that users tended to overrate their test performance. [13] On modafinil, Wikipedia describes research in well-rested people as mixed. [12] Piracetam reviews cited on Wikipedia found insufficient evidence for dementia and no evidence for ADHD when used alone. [11]

Academic ethics discussions, such as the 2008 Nature commentary by Greely and colleagues listed on Wikipedia, address responsible use of such drugs by healthy people. [1] In 2016 the AMA discouraged prescribing nootropics to healthy people, citing variable, dose-dependent and modest effects. [1]

Reported concerns include side effects, psychological dependence with stimulant-type agents, missing long-term safety data and products that contain undeclared drugs. [1][5] The FDA sent warning letters to nootropic sellers beginning in 2010, and in February 2019 the FDA and FTC jointly warned about advertising claims. [1] Studies by Cohen and colleagues found piracetam in supplements sold in the US (2020), five unapproved drugs in cognitive supplements (2021) and meclofenoxate (2022). [1] Modafinil side effects include headache, nausea, anxiety and insomnia, with rare serious skin reactions, and it is contraindicated in some cardiac conditions and pregnancy. [12] Piracetam reports include anxiety, insomnia, irritability and headache. [11]

US outlets covered nootropics as a Silicon Valley trend around 2015 to 2017. Marketplace quoted UC Berkeley nutritional scientist Marc Hellerstein as doubting effectiveness, saying claims rarely rest on studies medical researchers would accept. [14] The same piece notes that because these products are sold as supplements, the FDA does not review them as it does drugs. [14]

Human studies include reviews of cognitive enhancers in healthy people and in university students, a systematic review of plant-derived nootropics, and trials of individual products such as a randomized trial of guayusa and lion's mane extracts and one of an energy drink in gamers. [2][5][7][8][9] Studies of full stacks as assembled on forums were not found.

lore.intro: Nootropics are discussed on looksmax.org as tools for studying and motivation, often with competing views on prescription versus over-the-counter options. [3][4][15]

claims.claim: Prescription stimulants work and over-the-counter nootropics are 'cope'
claims.believers: One user says OTC stimulants give only slight energy with side effects and recommends a prescription instead. [4]
claims.experts: Reviews report dose-dependent effects for stimulants in healthy people and limited evidence for most supplements. [1][5]

claims.claim: A stack of supplements can improve focus for exams
claims.believers: A forum reply lists a multi-supplement stack and a caffeine-theanine pairing for studying. [3]
claims.experts: A systematic review of plant-derived nootropics found effects in some cognitive domains for Bacopa, Ginkgo and caffeine, with inconsistencies. [7]

claims.believers: A user building a study stack lists modafinil as a core item. [15]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes research in well-rested people as mixed, and cognitive-enhancer reviews report users overrating their performance. [12][13]

claims.claim: Piracetam and other racetams boost cognition in healthy people
claims.believers: Racetams are a standard entry in forum stack lists. [15]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports little evidence that racetams enhance cognition in people without impairment, and low toxicity. [1][11]

claims.claim: Some nootropics should be avoided because they affect hair or growth hormone
claims.believers: A poster says they will avoid anything linked to BDNF and hair loss or to HGH and IGF-1. [15]
claims.experts: No published studies were found that test these concerns for the stacks as used on forums.

claims.claim: Over-the-counter supplements are what they say on the label
claims.believers: Users who prefer supplements treat them as the safe option. [15]
claims.experts: Studies by Cohen and colleagues found unapproved drugs in some cognitive supplements, and the FDA has issued warning letters. [1]

claims.claim: Better focus translates into better looks through habits
claims.believers: Users frame concentration as the missing piece for consistent routines. [3]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested whether stacks change grooming, training or skin-care adherence.
